title: How To Teach In The AI Era
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Citing reporting on widespread AI-assisted cheating from middle school through college, Linsin proposes a concrete three-part lesson structure meant to protect the skills AI erodes — critical thinking, academic grit, complex problem solving, and original expression. Part one strips all electronics from the lesson entirely, requiring students to take notes with pencil and paper as in a pre-digital classroom. Part two demands a genuinely compelling, expertise-driven lesson from the teacher, since the structure only works if students actually want to engage with the material being taught live. Part three shifts all the real work — writing the essay, solving the problem, running the experiment — into class time with no internet access, closing off any opportunity to outsource the task to AI afterward. His central claim is that the goal isn't banning AI outright or trying to out-compete students at using it (he concedes they're already better at it than most teachers), but rather constraining its use enough to preserve the deeper capacities that come from direct, unaided engagement with hard material.
points: Part one of the structure removes all electronics, requiring pencil-and-paper notetaking during the lesson itself.
Part two requires a genuinely compelling, expertise-driven lesson, since the whole structure depends on real student engagement.
Part three moves all actual work into class time with no internet access, eliminating the chance to outsource it to AI afterward.
The goal is explicitly not banning AI outright, but constraining its use enough to protect critical thinking, grit, and original expression.
quotes: According to a recent article in New York magazine, nearly every student is using AI to cheat their way through college.
Teaching students how to use AI is for the most part also a waste of time. They’re already way better at it than you.
Remove all electronics. This means no access to laptops or phones for the entire lesson.
No internet. No “research.” No cheating. Just, let’s see what you got.
With the right leadership and teaching skills, kids still love to learn and solve problems. This will never change. It’s ingrained in their DNA.
It just means that you’ll constrain its use to ensure them the best and most well-rounded education.
